opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we've spent a lot of time on, because the economics drive so much of how people actually build these systems.

The way I frame it is that there are really two costs, not one. There's the direct cost: what you pay per image or per box. And there's the downstream cost: what happens to your model's performance when you train on those labels. People tend to fixate on the first and forget the second.

On the direct cost, it's not even close. Human annotation, especially for dense tasks like bounding boxes or segmentation masks, is slow and expensive. You're paying for people's time, for quality-control passes, and for the iteration loop when the labeling guidelines turn out to be ambiguous. Running a strong off-the-shelf foundation model, an open-vocabulary detector or a segmentation model, over the same dataset costs a tiny fraction of that in compute and finishes in hours instead of weeks. We're talking orders of magnitude in both dollars and time.

The more interesting question is the downstream one. Do models trained on auto-generated labels perform as well as models trained on human labels? What we've found is that, for a lot of common categories and fairly standard settings, they get surprisingly close. Sometimes they're comparable. One reason is that human labels aren't the pristine ground truth we pretend they are. They have their own noise, inconsistencies between annotators, and missed objects. So you're not comparing a perfect label to a noisy one. You're comparing two different noise profiles.

There's a subtlety, though, around confidence thresholds. If you only keep the model's very high-confidence predictions, you get precise labels but you miss a lot of objects, and the downstream model learns to under-detect. A more moderate threshold that accepts some false positives in exchange for better recall often works better for training. That's somewhat counterintuitive.

Where auto-labeling still struggles is the long tail: rare classes, unusual viewpoints, domain-specific stuff like medical or industrial imagery where foundation models haven't seen much. That's where human expertise is still worth paying for.

So my practical takeaway is that it isn't human versus model. Let the model do the bulk of the labeling cheaply, then spend your human budget surgically: on verification, on the hard and rare cases, and on building a really good evaluation set. That hybrid approach captures most of the cost savings without giving up the quality where it matters.

r001.rationale: The response separates direct annotation costs from downstream model-performance costs, but it does not distinguish labeling cost from the cost of running the full research experiment.

r002.rationale: It says model labeling is much cheaper, but does not state that quantifying this expected gap has scientific value even when its direction is unsurprising.

r003.rationale: The response ties the cost savings to label quality: it discusses downstream performance on auto-generated labels and recommends a hybrid approach to capture savings without sacrificing quality where it matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I actually think it's one of the most important and least examined questions in the field right now. The way the cost comparison is usually framed is kind of naive. It's: a human labeler costs X dollars an hour, and a model labels for essentially free once it's trained, so obviously you want to push as much of the labeling onto the model as possible. And on the surface that's true. But I think it hides a lot.

The first thing it hides is that the costs aren't measured in the same units. Human labeling is expensive up front, but you're buying something fairly well understood. You know roughly what the error profile looks like, you can audit it, you can send it back. Model-generated labels are cheap at the margin, but you're inheriting whatever biases and blind spots that model has, and those errors are correlated. If a human labeler is tired, they make a random mistake. If a model has a systematic failure on, say, small objects or unusual lighting, it makes that mistake on every single frame, and now that's baked into your training set. So the cheap labels can actually be more expensive downstream, because you've contaminated the thing you were trying to build.

The second thing is that in my experience, the interesting part of the cost isn't the labeling itself, it's the verification. We did some work looking at this in video, where the volume is just enormous. You can't have a human draw boxes on every frame, that's never going to happen. So you propagate, you use models, you use tracking. But then the question becomes, how much human attention do I need to spend to actually trust the result? And that's where the real economics live. The cost of a human checking a label is way lower than the cost of a human producing one from scratch, but it's not zero, and it scales with how much you distrust the model.

So the way I've come to think about it is less "human versus model" and more as a budget allocation problem. You've got a fixed amount of human attention, which is your scarce resource, and the model's job is to spend that attention as efficiently as possible. Point the human at the frames, or the examples, where the model is uncertain, or where the stakes are high, or where you suspect the systematic error is going to show up. If you do that well, the human labeling and the model labeling aren't competing, they're complementary, and the question of which is cheaper kind of dissolves.

And honestly, I'll say one more thing, which is that I think we as a research community underweight the value of just looking at the data. A lot of the labeling cost discussion is about getting labels at scale. But some of the biggest improvements I've seen in a project came from somebody sitting down and actually looking at a few hundred examples carefully, not because they were labeling them, but because they understood what the problem actually was. That's a cost nobody puts in the spreadsheet, and I think it's the one that matters most.

r001.rationale: The response discusses labeling and verification costs but does not distinguish them from the cost of running the full research experiment.

r002.rationale: It calls the cost comparison important and underexamined, but does not state that quantifying the gap has scientific value even if the expected direction is unsurprising.

r003.rationale: It explains that model labels can be cheap initially yet more costly downstream when their errors or biases contaminate the data, making the cost advantage depend on label quality.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to compare the cost of getting to a useful level of quality, rather than just the cost of producing a label. With human labeling, there’s the time spent doing the annotation, but also reviewing it and resolving disagreements. With model-generated labels, there’s the cost of running the model, and then the question of how much human correction those labels need.

So a cheap prediction isn’t necessarily a cheap annotation. If a person has to spend a lot of time fixing it, you may not have saved much. The interesting research question is where the model can reduce human effort and where it should ask for help. I’d want to compare those approaches at the same quality level, accounting for the full amount of human work involved.

r001.rationale: The response compares human annotation and model-labeling costs, but does not distinguish those costs from the cost of running the full research experiment.

r002.rationale: It calls finding where models reduce human effort an interesting research question, but does not say that measuring the cost gap has scientific value even if its direction is unsurprising.

r003.rationale: The response says costs should be compared at the same quality level and notes that human correction can erase savings from a cheap prediction, making the value of the cost advantage dependent on label quality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is to compare the total cost of getting labels that are useful, rather than just the cost of producing a label. With human labeling, you have the annotation time, but you also have training, quality control, and resolving disagreements. With model-generated labels, you have the cost of running the model, but you still need some way to assess whether those labels are good enough.

So the question becomes: where is the human effort most valuable? If a model can handle the straightforward examples and a person can focus on correcting mistakes or resolving ambiguity, that can be a much more efficient use of the budget. But a cheap label that introduces errors and hurts the downstream model isn’t necessarily cheap. You really want to measure the cost against the performance you ultimately get.

r001.rationale: It compares the costs of producing useful labels, but does not distinguish labeling costs from the cost of running the full research experiment.

r002.rationale: It does not say that quantifying the expected human-versus-model cost gap has scientific value, regardless of whether its direction is surprising.

r003.rationale: It says cheap model labels may introduce errors and hurt downstream performance, so their cost advantage must be judged in light of label quality.
